summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol handles contacts, meaning individuals or organizations with social information identifiers, in a shared registry. It specifies command syntax and semantics for contact objects. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5733 defines how EPP registries store and manage contact records. A record can include names, addresses, phone numbers, email, transfer authorization, and preferences about disclosure.

subtitle: The EPP mapping for contact records, their registration details, disclosure choices, and transfers.

tldr.problem: A shared registry needs a consistent record for the people or organizations associated with registered objects, including how their details may be disclosed.
tldr.mechanism: The contact mapping defines XML fields for identity, postal information, phone, email, authorization information, and disclosure preferences, with EPP commands to manage the record.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5733 is an Internet Standard that replaces RFC 4933. Its authorization information must be protected because it can permit transfers or release of information.

today: RFC 5733 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4933. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The EPP Contact Mapping
sections.content:
RFC 5733 defines an XML mapping for managing individual or organizational contact records in a shared repository. It applies version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) and relies on the base command structures in RFC 5730.

Each contact has a server-unique identifier. The sponsoring client and the server can view and modify its attributes, subject to the mapping's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact object is a registry record for a person, role, or organization. The mapping specifies how EPP clients create, inspect, change, transfer, and remove the record.

sections.title: Contact Details and Status
sections.content:
A contact record has postal-address information, including a city and country identifier. It can include one internationalized address form and one localized form. Names and addresses can use UTF-8, while the internationalized form is limited to text representable in 7-bit US-ASCII.

Telephone numbers begin with a plus sign, a country code, a dot, and the number's digits; an optional attribute holds an extension. The record also has status values, which indicate restrictions, links to other objects, or pending actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact record holds identity and postal details, with optional phone, fax, and email fields. It can store address information in forms suited to different character sets.

sections.title: Client Preferences for Disclosure
sections.content:
The contact:disclose element lets a client identify contact fields that need exceptional handling under the server's announced data-collection policy. Its flag says whether the specified fields may be disclosed as an exception to that policy.

The element must name at least one field, such as a name, address, telephone number, or email. The server must reject a request that conflicts with its announced policy using error 2308. Access to fields can also depend on the querying client's identity and authorization information.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can state whether selected contact fields may be disclosed under the server's policy. The server rejects preferences that conflict with that policy.

sections.title: EPP Commands for Contacts
sections.content:
check asks whether an identifier can be provisioned, and info retrieves a contact's details. create requires an identifier, postal information, an email address, and authorization information. update changes contact fields, status, or disclosure settings.

delete should not remove a contact that remains associated with other objects. Unlike the host mapping, this contact mapping defines a transfer command for changing sponsorship; it does not define a renewal command.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP provides commands to check, read, create, update, delete, and transfer contact records. A contact should not be deleted while other registry objects still refer to it.

sections.title: Contact Transfers and Review
sections.content:
A contact transfer request includes the contact identifier and its authorization information. A transfer query reports the request's status and the clients involved.

A server may pause a transform command for human or third-party review. It returns code 1001, marks the contact with a pending status, and later sends a service message stating whether the request was approved or denied. Unauthorized transform requests must be rejected with code 2201.
sections.plainLanguage: Authorization information is used when a client requests a contact transfer. A registry may hold a request for review and later notify the clients of its decision.

sections.title: Protecting Authorization Information
sections.content:
Authorization information is required to create a contact and may be used for query and transfer operations. If it is disclosed, an unauthorized party may be able to transfer the contact or obtain information.

Both client and server must store and exchange authorization information using high-grade encryption. The mapping adds no other security services beyond the base EPP protocol and its underlying layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization value can help a client transfer a contact, so it must be kept private. The mapping relies on EPP and its transport layers for other security protections.
